questions.prompt: What primary performance advantage does CRTP offer over virtual dispatch when all concrete types are known at compile time?
options: CRTP lets you store unrelated derived types inside a single std::vector<Base>
Calls resolve statically via static_cast with no vptr memory overhead, no vtable lookup, and full inlining
CRTP moves object construction onto the stack automatically
CRTP allows overriding private virtual functions without virtual destructors
questions.explanation: Because Base<Derived> knows the concrete Derived type at compile time, static_cast<Derived&>(*this) resolves calls statically, eliminating the hidden vptr per object and enabling inline optimization.

questions.prompt: What problem does C++23's explicit object parameter `(this auto&& self)` solve directly inside a lambda expression?
options: It makes the lambda capture local variables by move automatically
It turns the lambda into a virtual function callable through a base pointer
It evaluates every call to the lambda as consteval
It lets the lambda call itself recursively without std::function or passing itself as an extra argument
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.fct] and [expr.prim.lambda], naming an explicit object parameter `this auto&& self` binds `self` to the lambda's closure object, enabling direct, zero-overhead recursion.

questions.prompt: Why does the member function `Widget::read` below fail to compile in C++23?
options: Inside an explicit object member function there is no implicit `this` pointer; it must write `self.count`
An explicit object parameter cannot be const-qualified as `const Widget&`
Explicit object member functions must be templates
Members cannot be accessed inside explicit object functions unless declared mutable
questions.explanation: Under [expr.prim.this] and [class.mfct], `this` is not in scope as an expression inside an explicit object member function body. All member access must go explicitly through the named parameter `self` (`self.count`).

questions.prompt: What is the exact type of `fn` when taking the address of explicit object member function `Counter::bump`?
options: void (Counter::*)()
void (Counter::*)(Counter&)
void (*)(Counter&)
Ill-formed: you cannot take the address of an explicit object member function
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.fct] and [expr.unary.op], an explicit object member function behaves like a non-member function for pointer formation: `&Counter::bump` yields a plain function pointer `void (*)(Counter&)`, not a pointer-to-member-function.

questions.prompt: Which declaration of an explicit object member function is legal in C++23?
options: virtual void draw(this Shape& self);
void draw(this const Shape& self) noexcept;
void draw(this Shape& self) const;
static void draw(this Shape& self);
questions.explanation: Under [dcl.fct], a function declaration with an explicit object parameter cannot be `virtual`, `static`, cv-qualified (`const`/`volatile`), or ref-qualified (`&`/`&&`)—those properties belong on the explicit object parameter itself. Exception specifications like `noexcept` remain valid.

questions.prompt: In `Box` below, why does `std::move(b).bad()` yield `std::string&` instead of `std::string&&`, whereas `std::move(b).good()` yields `std::string&&`?
options: std::forward<Self>(self) ignores template deduction when Self is an explicit object parameter
Member access on a template always decays rvalues to lvalues
std::forward_like forces a copy of item onto the stack
Under [expr.ref], accessing a reference member `E1.m` where `m` is `T&` produces an lvalue even when `E1` is an rvalue, whereas `std::forward_like<Self>` applies Self's value category onto `item`
questions.explanation: By [expr.ref], member access on an rvalue yields an xvalue only for non-reference, non-static data members; when the member itself is an lvalue reference (`std::string&`), `E1.item` stays an lvalue. `std::forward_like<Self>(self.item)` transfers `Self`'s constness and value category onto `item` ([forward]).
